Indian Geography - Class Notes | 16 November 2026

Topics: the summer (hot weather) season, continued: the storms of the season - dust storms, thunderstorms (with lightning and hail) and tropical cyclones (formation, structure, IMD classification, tracks and landfall, Bay of Bengal versus Arabian Sea, warnings and naming, climate change, and the major cyclones of 2023-2026 including Cyclone Akvan now in the Bay of Bengal); a comparison of the storms; and the regional rainfall pattern of India (sources of rain, controls, the four IMD regions, and why the rain differs from region to region).

Class date: 16 November 2026. This class continues the summer season from the 15 November note (section 4), which covered temperature, the loo, local storms, heat waves and heat-wave policy, and builds on the monsoon mechanism notes of 13 November and 14 November. Sections, maps, figures and correction ids restart at 1.

Labels: [Correction] marks a substantive change to the rough notes; [Additional] marks relevant supporting material; [Verification Required] flags claims that could not be confirmed; [Current Affairs] marks dated news (as of 17 November 2026); † marks a standard fact not re-checked against a page opened for this note. Maps are schematic (simplified Natural Earth data) and diagrams are conceptual. Time-sensitive figures carry their year and source.

1. Storms of the Hot Weather Season: the Common Idea

The notes list the storms of March-May as dust storms, thunderstorms, hailstorms and cyclonic (tropical) storms. They differ in size and fuel, but share one idea: each is a low-pressure (LP) system with fast winds, rising air and, usually, moist and cloudy or rainy conditions.

Strong heating of land or warm sea → air near the surface becomes light, unstable → air rises; pressure falls (LP) → surrounding air rushes in = fast winds → rising moist air cools, condenses = clouds, rain → latent heat released keeps the air rising
  • Why the hot season: by April-May the land of north and central India is very hot, the air near the ground is unstable, and moist air from the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea starts to reach the land. Heat plus moisture plus a trigger (a trough, a late western disturbance, sea breeze or hills) gives convection.
  • Three scales: a thunderstorm cell is a few kilometres across and lasts about an hour†; a dust storm can sweep across several districts; a tropical cyclone is several hundred kilometres wide and lasts several days.
  • Where: dust storms in the dry north-west; thunderstorms in the moist east, north-east and south (and in central India); cyclones over the warm Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea (Map 1).
[Additional] Instability in one line. Air is unstable when a parcel pushed upward stays warmer (lighter) than the air around it and keeps rising. Strong surface heating and moisture make air unstable; a warm layer aloft (an inversion, or the "lid" of an upper-air high) makes it stable. This is why the same May heat gives thunderstorms in moist Bengal but only hot, dry loo and dust in Rajasthan, where the air is dry and capped by sinking air above (see the heat dome, 15 November note 4.4).

2. Dust Storms (Andhi)

2.1 What and Where

  • What: a strong, gusty wind that lifts loose sand and dust into a moving wall, cutting visibility sharply. The notes call it a "blind storm" because people and vehicles cannot see. Locally it is called andhi ("blinding").
  • Where: the Thar desert and its margins - west Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and west Uttar Pradesh - and the dry Kutch region. Dust is often carried far east over the Indo-Gangetic plain.
  • When: mainly April to June, the hottest and driest months before the monsoon arrives.
  • Weather: a sudden squall, a drop in temperature and, sometimes, a few drops or light rain at the end (the "mild rains" of the notes).

2.2 How a Dust Storm Forms

Intense heating of dry, bare ground → surface heat low; very unstable but dry air → a trigger: a trough, a late WD or a passing thunderstorm → strong winds or a cold downdraft hit the ground and spread out (gust front) → loose, dry soil lifted = wall of dust
  • Two common types: (1) convective dust storms - the cold downdraft of a dry thunderstorm spreads out at the ground as a gust front and raises a dust wall; (2) pressure-gradient dust storms - a steep pressure difference (for example, behind a western disturbance) drives strong, dusty winds over a wide area for hours.
  • Why the Thar: loose sand and silt, almost no vegetation, dry soil, intense heating and low humidity. Ploughed, dry fields after the rabi harvest add dust.
  • Why little rain: the air below the cloud base is so dry that most rain evaporates before it reaches the ground. This evaporation cools the falling air and makes the downdraft even stronger - the reason dust storms can be violent.
[Correction] The notes say "an LP system develops near the Thar" and causes the dust storm. The surface heat low over north-west India and Pakistan is the background, but a dust storm is not itself a separate low-pressure system like a depression. It is a wind event: a thunderstorm's cold downdraft (gust front) or a strong pressure-gradient wind lifting dry soil. Keep "LP system" for depressions and cyclones.

2.3 Impacts

  • Harm: deaths and injuries from collapsing walls, hoardings and trees and from lightning in dust-thunderstorms (for example the deadly storms of early May 2018 in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh†); damage to power lines and standing crops; road, rail and air disruption; very high PM10 pollution and breathing problems.
  • Some benefits: a short break from the heat; dust carries nutrients that settle on soils and oceans.
  • Climate link [Additional]: dust and other aerosols over the Indo-Gangetic plain absorb and scatter sunlight and can change pre-monsoon heating and rainfall; their net effect on the monsoon is still debated (see the 14 November note on air pollution and the monsoon).

3. Thunderstorms, Lightning and Hail

3.1 What and Where

  • What: a storm from a towering cumulonimbus (Cb) cloud with lightning and thunder, gusty winds, heavy showers and sometimes hail. It is a small, local, convective low-pressure system.
  • When: in India the pre-monsoon season (March-May) is the main thunderstorm season; the showers are called pre-monsoon showers or thundershowers. Thunderstorms also occur during the monsoon and in October-November.
  • Where: most frequent in eastern and north-eastern India (West Bengal, Odisha, Jharkhand, Bihar, Assam) and in Kerala and Karnataka; also common over central India, and in the north-west as dust-thunderstorms.
[Correction] The notes place thunderstorms "in eastern India and south India". Those are the wettest thunderstorm belts, but thunderstorms and lightning are widespread: central India has many, and the north-west has dust-thunderstorms and hail. In 2023 the state with the most lightning deaths was Madhya Pradesh (397), ahead of Bihar (345), Odisha (294), Uttar Pradesh (287) and Jharkhand (194) (NCRB data via Down To Earth).

3.2 How a Thunderstorm Forms: Three Stages

Conditions: (1) moisture in the lower air; (2) unstable air (strong surface heating); and (3) a lifting trigger - daytime heating, a trough or front, converging winds or hills.

  1. Cumulus (developing) stage: warm, moist air rises in updrafts, cools and condenses. The latent heat of condensation keeps the cloud warmer than its surroundings, so it keeps growing upward. Little or no rain yet.
  2. Mature stage: the cloud becomes a cumulonimbus reaching the tropopause, where it spreads out as an anvil. Falling rain drags air down, so updrafts and downdrafts exist side by side. This is the stage of heavy rain, hail, lightning, thunder and a squall when the cold downdraft spreads out at the ground as a gust front.
  3. Dissipating stage: downdrafts take over and cut off the supply of warm, moist air; rain becomes light and the cloud thins out.

3.3 Lightning and Thunder

  • Charge separation: inside the Cb cloud, collisions between rising ice crystals and falling soft hail (graupel) separate electric charge. Usually the upper cloud becomes positive and the lower cloud negative†.
  • Lightning is a giant electric discharge within a cloud, between clouds, or between the cloud and the ground (the dangerous one).
  • Thunder is the sound of the air heated suddenly by lightning - to about 30,000°C† - which expands explosively and sends out a shock wave. It is not caused by clouds colliding (PYQ 2, Prelims 2013). Light travels faster than sound, so we see the flash before we hear the thunder.
  • Who dies: mostly farmers and outdoor workers in rural areas, often while sheltering under isolated trees.

3.4 Hailstorms

  • How hail forms: very strong updrafts carry raindrops above the freezing level, where they freeze; they fall, are lifted again and gain layers of ice, until they are too heavy for the updraft and fall as hailstones.
  • Where and when in India: mostly February-May, in north-west and central India and Maharashtra (Vidarbha, Marathwada), often with late western disturbances†. Hail flattens ripening rabi crops (wheat, gram, mustard) and fruit orchards.

3.6 Lightning as a Disaster

  • Scale: lightning is India's biggest natural killer among the "forces of nature" in NCRB data: 2,558 deaths in 2023, about 39.7% of 6,444 such deaths, ahead of heat/sun stroke (about 806) and cold (733) (Down To Earth, 30 September 2025). Earlier years: 2,357 (2018), 2,876 (2019), 2,862 (2020), 2,880 (2021) and 2,887 (2022) (Ground Report, citing NCRB).
  • Rising strikes: the Climate Resilient Observing Systems Promotion Council (CROPC) reports a 400% rise in lightning strikes between 2019-20 and 2024-25, and studies suggest roughly 8-10% more lightning for every 1°C of warming. [Verification Required] These are CROPC and media figures; the 400% rise partly reflects better detection networks.
  • Tools: IMD lightning and thunderstorm nowcasts; the Damini app (IITM Pune) for lightning alerts; the Sachet common-alerting app; NDMA guidelines; the CROPC-IMD Lightning Resilient India Campaign; lightning arresters and safe shelters in schools and villages.
[Pictorial Representation Recommended: a lightning-density (flashes per km² per year) map of India with the NCRB 2023 lightning-death states overlaid, to show that central and eastern India combine frequent lightning with high exposure; suggested source: CROPC-IMD Annual Lightning Report or IITM Pune lightning network.]
[Correction] The notes say lightning is "now included as part of national disaster". As with heat waves, lightning (and heat waves) were added to the list of notified natural calamities eligible for SDRF/NDRF funding in the operational guidelines for 2026-31, following the 16th Finance Commission. India has no separate legal category called a "national disaster". Details in the 15 November note, 4.6.

4. Tropical Cyclones (Cyclonic Storms)

A tropical cyclone is an intense, warm-core low-pressure system that forms over a warm tropical ocean, with winds spiralling inward (anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere) and very heavy rain. It brings some of the fastest sustained winds on the earth's surface. The same storm is called a cyclone in the Indian Ocean, a hurricane in the Atlantic and east Pacific, a typhoon in the west Pacific and a willy-willy near north-west Australia†.

[Additional] The notes call cyclones "one of the fastest winds on the surface". That is right for large, long-lived systems; the very highest winds on earth occur in tornadoes, which are tiny and last minutes. A tropical cyclone is different from the temperate (extra-tropical) cyclones of the mid-latitudes, such as the western disturbances, which form along fronts and draw energy from contrasting air masses rather than from latent heat (see the comparison in section 5).

4.1 Conditions for Formation

  1. A large, warm sea surface: NCERT gives a sea-surface temperature above 27°C; the scientific threshold usually quoted is about 26.5°C, through the top ~50 m of the ocean†. The notes' "approx. 27°C" matches NCERT.
  2. Coriolis force: needed to set the inflowing air spinning. It is zero at the equator, so cyclones rarely form within about 5° of the equator†.
  3. Low vertical wind shear: the wind must not change much in speed and direction with height, or the storm's tower is torn apart.
  4. A pre-existing disturbance: a weak low or low-level cyclonic circulation, often in or near the ITCZ or the monsoon trough.
  5. High humidity in the middle troposphere, and upper-level divergence (outflow aloft) that removes the rising air.

NCERT Class 11 Fundamentals of Physical Geography, chapter on atmospheric circulation and weather systems†.

[Additional] Cyclones near the equator. The notes say cyclones now form "near the equator despite less Coriolis force". Formation very close to the equator is still rare, but there are striking cases: Senyar (November 2025) was the first recorded cyclone to form in the Strait of Malacca, near 5°N, and caused deadly floods in Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia (2025 season summary; IMD review in MAUSAM 2026). An IITM study found that in the Arabian Sea, cyclones in 2001-2019 formed more often at lower latitudes (below 8°N), which gives them a longer life over warm water (Deshpande et al., 2021).

4.2 Source of Energy and Structure

Warm sea evaporates water → moist air spirals in towards the low → rises in the eyewall, cools, condenses (water vapour → droplets) → latent heat of condensation released → warm core, air rises faster, surface pressure falls further → stronger inflow and winds (self-feeding loop)
  • The notes' "heat-releasing process" is the release of latent heat of condensation: the heat absorbed when sea water evaporated is given back to the air when the vapour condenses. This is the engine of a tropical cyclone; it creates the intense low pressure and hence the fast winds.
  • Structure: the eye (calm, clear, sinking warm air, lowest pressure, about 20-50 km across†); the eyewall (a ring of the tallest Cb clouds with the strongest winds and heaviest rain); spiral rain bands; inflow near the surface and outflow aloft.
  • The eye is warmer than its surroundings (a warm core), not cooler (PYQ 3).
  • Decay: a cyclone weakens over land (moisture supply cut, more friction) or cooler water, or in strong wind shear. So "the more time over warm ocean, the worse the cyclone", as the notes say.

4.3 Stages and IMD Classification

A tropical cyclone starts as a low-pressure area and, if conditions stay favourable, deepens step by step. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) classifies the systems over the North Indian Ocean by the maximum sustained surface wind averaged over three minutes (at 10 m height).

Severe cyclonic storm (SCS)89-11748-63
Very severe cyclonic storm (VSCS)118-16664-89

Source: IMD Pune Hazard Atlas - Cyclone (older 7-step version) and the current 8-step scale as used in Deshpande et al. (2021), Table 1 and in IMD bulletins. Super cyclones on record: Odisha 1999, Gonu 2007, Kyarr 2019, Amphan 2020†.

[Correction] The notes give "normal cyclone 62-87, severe 88-117, very strong 89-167, extremely severe 168-". The correct IMD bands are Cyclonic storm 62-88, Severe cyclonic storm 89-117, Very severe 118-166, Extremely severe 167-221 and Super cyclonic storm 222 km/h and above. The notes' "very strong 89-167" overlaps the severe band and misses the super cyclonic storm category. (Some IMD documents round the extremely severe lower limit to 168 km/h; the knot value, 90 kt, is the same.)
[Correction] The notes say a cyclonic storm needs winds above 61 km/h "for more than 3 min". The 3 minutes is the averaging period used to measure the sustained wind, not a minimum duration of the storm. The US agencies use a 1-minute average, so their figures for the same storm are higher; neither is wrong.

4.4 Track, Landfall and Storm Surge

  • Track: cyclones are steered by the larger winds around them. In the tropics the easterlies on the southern side of the subtropical high push them from east to west; they then turn north-west or north, and many in the Bay of Bengal recurve north-east towards Odisha, West Bengal, Bangladesh or Myanmar when they meet the westerlies (Map 1, Map 2). This is the notes' "east to west, then northward".
  • Landfall: the moment the centre (eye) crosses the coast. The coast near landfall gets the worst of three hazards: destructive winds, very heavy rain and river floods, and the storm surge.
  • Storm surge: an abnormal rise of the sea, caused mainly by strong onshore winds piling water against the coast (plus a small rise from the low pressure). Over a shallow, funnel-shaped coast such as the head of the Bay of Bengal, the surge is higher and penetrates far inland up the deltas. Historically, most cyclone deaths in this region came from surge flooding, not wind†.
  • Fujiwhara effect [Additional]: when two cyclones come close (roughly within 1,400 km†), they rotate around a common centre, can change each other's track and speed, and the stronger may absorb the weaker. Asked in Mains 2026 (PYQ 8).

4.5 Why the Bay of Bengal Gets More (and Deadlier) Cyclones than the Arabian Sea

Climatologically, cyclone activity in the Bay of Bengal is about four times that of the Arabian Sea (Deshpande et al., 2021, citing Dube et al. 1997).

FactorBay of BengalArabian Sea
Sea-surface temperatureWarmer, and stays warmCooler; upwelling off Somalia and Oman in summer
Fresh water from riversGanga-Brahmaputra, Irrawaddy and others form a light, fresh surface layer that resists mixing, so the surface stays warm under a stormFew large rivers; saltier, better-mixed water
Seed disturbancesRemnants of west Pacific typhoons and lows crossing from the South China Sea and Andaman SeaFewer seed lows
Upper airLower wind shear in transition seasonsDry air from Arabia and stronger shear
Shape and coastFunnel shape, shallow shelf, low and crowded deltas: higher surges, more deathsSteeper coast; many storms move to Oman, Yemen or Pakistan, or die at sea
[Correction] The notes say the Bay of Bengal suits cyclones "due to the smaller size and receiving more rivers". The rivers part is right (fresh-water layer keeps the surface warm). Size is not the reason; the key factors are the warmer water, the river-made fresh layer, the supply of seed disturbances from the east, lower wind shear, and the funnel shape that makes landfalls more deadly.

4.6 Cyclone Seasons over India

  • Two peaks (bimodal): pre-monsoon (April-May, early June) and post-monsoon (October-December). The post-monsoon peak is the more active, and most of India's deadliest cyclones struck then†.
  • Why few in July-September: the strong monsoon flow (low-level westerlies under the upper-level tropical easterly jet) creates high vertical wind shear. The Bay produces many monsoon depressions but few cyclones. In 2026 the monsoon had 14 low-pressure systems, including 6 depressions, but no cyclonic storm (IMD, 30 September 2026).
  • Exceptions: Asna (late August 2024) formed over land near Kutch and moved into the Arabian Sea, a very rare monsoon-season cyclone†.
[Correction] The notes say cyclones are "also coming till early December" as a climate-change sign. October-December is the normal post-monsoon cyclone season, so December cyclones are not new (recent ones: Michaung, December 2023; Fengal, late November-early December 2024; Ditwah, late November-early December 2025). [Verification Required] No source was found showing that December cyclones are becoming more frequent.

4.7 Mitigation: Warning, Naming and Preparedness

  • RSMC New Delhi: IMD is the WMO Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre - Tropical Cyclones, New Delhi, responsible for tracking, naming and warning for the North Indian Ocean (Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea, about 45°E-100°E). Worldwide there are six RSMCs for tropical cyclones (Miami, Honolulu, Tokyo, New Delhi, La Reunion and Nadi) and five Tropical Cyclone Warning Centres†.
  • Tools: satellites (INSAT-3DS is used in current advisories), Doppler weather radars, ocean buoys, the Dvorak technique (T-numbers) and numerical models. IMD's average track-forecast errors have fallen sharply over the past two decades†.
  • Four-stage warning for the coast: Pre-cyclone watch (about 72 hours ahead), Cyclone alert (48 hours), Cyclone warning (24 hours) and Post-landfall outlook. In current IMD bulletins the cyclone alert goes out as an Orange message (Akvan, 17 November 2026) and the cyclone warning as a Red message (Remal, 26 May 2024).
  • Colour codes (impact-based): Green - no warning; Yellow - be updated (watch); Orange - be prepared; Red - take action (asked in Mains 2022, PYQ 6).
  • Naming (since 2004): names come from the WMO/ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones. The panel had 8 members in 2004 and now has 13: Bangladesh, India, Iran, Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, UAE and Yemen. The 2020 list has 169 names (13 from each country)†, arranged in columns by country in alphabetical order of country names and used in sequence; a used name is not reused. A system is named when it becomes a cyclonic storm (62 km/h).
  • Why name cyclones: easier to remember and communicate than numbers, less confusion when two systems exist at once, and better public response to warnings.
  • Preparedness on the ground: multipurpose cyclone shelters, evacuation plans and early-warning dissemination (the NDMA-led, World Bank-assisted National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project†), mangroves and shelterbelts (Sundarbans, Bhitarkanika), Coastal Regulation Zone rules, and community drills. Odisha's "zero-casualty" approach after the 1999 super cyclone is the model†.

4.8 Climate Change and Cyclones

  • Arabian Sea: an IITM study comparing 2001-2019 with 1982-2000 found a 52% rise in the frequency and an 80% rise in the duration of cyclonic storms over the Arabian Sea, and a 150% rise in the frequency of very severe cyclonic storms; Bay of Bengal cyclonic storms fell by 8% (Deshpande et al., 2021, Climate Dynamics; Nature Reviews Earth & Environment highlight). The rise is linked to warmer sea surface, more ocean heat content and more humid mid-level air. This supports the notes: "earlier very few cyclones in the Arabian Sea, now more".
  • Intensity and rainfall: warmer seas favour rapid intensification, more intense storms and heavier rain; a higher sea level makes every surge worse. The IPCC (AR6) assesses that the proportion of intense tropical cyclones has likely increased globally†.
  • New landfall places: cyclones such as Nisarga (June 2020, near Mumbai - the first June cyclone landfall on the Maharashtra coast on record) and Tauktae (May 2021) struck the west coast (Deshpande et al., 2021).
  • Caution: the total number of North Indian Ocean cyclones has not clearly increased; the change is in the Arabian Sea share, duration and intensity.
[Correction] The notes say "now more frequency of cyclones, led by global warming". This is true for the Arabian Sea (study above), but not for the North Indian Ocean as a whole: Bay of Bengal cyclonic storms fell slightly over the same period. Write "more and longer-lived Arabian Sea cyclones and more intense storms" rather than "more cyclones everywhere".

The name Akvan is from Iran's list†.

5.1 Model Answer: Major Storms of the Hot Weather Season and Their Differences

Introduction: March-May heats the Indian landmass and the seas around it, producing low-pressure systems of three scales: dust storms, thunderstorms and tropical cyclones.

Dust storms occur over the dry north-west. Intense heating of bare ground and a trigger (a gust front from a dry thunderstorm or a strong pressure gradient behind a western disturbance) lift loose soil into a wall of dust. There is little rain because the air is dry.

Thunderstorms need moisture, unstable air and a lifting trigger. They pass through cumulus, mature and dissipating stages. The mature cumulonimbus gives lightning, thunder, squalls, heavy showers and hail. Regional forms are Kalbaisakhi in Bengal and Odisha, Bardoli Chheerha in Assam, and mango and blossom showers in the south. Lightning is now India's largest natural killer.

Tropical cyclones are synoptic-scale, warm-core lows over seas warmer than about 26.5-27°C, driven by latent heat. They need Coriolis force, low wind shear and a seed disturbance. They peak in April-May and October-December, mostly in the Bay of Bengal, and cause destruction through wind, rain and storm surge.

Differences: they differ in scale (km to hundreds of km), life (minutes to days), energy source (dry convection, moist convection, latent heat over the sea), region (NW, E/NE/S, coasts) and hazard (visibility, lightning and hail, surge). Unlike all three, a western disturbance is an extra-tropical, frontal system.

Conclusion: all three are rising in impact - more lightning, more intense Arabian Sea cyclones - so impact-based early warning, lightning and cyclone shelters, and their inclusion in SDRF/NDRF (2026-31) are essential.

6. Rainfall Pattern of India (Regional Rainfall)

6.1 Sources of Rain through the Year

Season (IMD)Main source of rainShare of all-India annual rain (1971-2020 normal)
Winter (Jan-Feb)Western disturbances (NW India, Himalaya); some NE monsoon in the far southAbout 40 mm, ~3% (calculated as the remainder)
Pre-monsoon (Mar-May)Thunderstorms (nor-westers, mango and blossom showers), dust-thunderstorms, late WDs, pre-monsoon cyclones130.6 mm, ~11%
South-west monsoon (Jun-Sep)Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches; monsoon depressions868.6 mm, ~75%
Post-monsoon (Oct-Dec)NE monsoon (Tamil Nadu, south AP, Kerala); cyclones and depressions121.0 mm, ~10%
Annual1,160.1 mm

Source: IMD's new rainfall normals (1971-2020), reported by The Economic Times, 15 April 2022. The SW monsoon share is 74.9%; the winter figure is the annual total minus the other three seasons. Tamil Nadu is the exception: it gets about 48% of its annual rain in October-December and only 36% in June-September.

6.2 Why South-west Monsoon Rain Differs from Place to Place

  • Distance from the sea: the farther inland, the less moisture is left (the Arabian Sea branch weakens towards the interior; the Bay branch weakens up the Ganga valley).
  • Relief (physiography): mountains across the wind force air up and give orographic rain on the windward side and a rain shadow on the leeward side (Western Ghats, Meghalaya plateau, Himalayan foothills).
  • Direction of the wind relative to the relief: winds hitting a range at right angles give heavy rain; winds blowing parallel to a range or a coast give little (the Aravalli, the Coromandel coast).
  • Position of the monsoon trough (the ITCZ over land): the trough runs from north-west India to the head of the Bay. When it lies over the plains the monsoon is active; when it moves to the Himalayan foothills there is a break in the plains and heavy rain in the hills.
  • Low-pressure systems: monsoon depressions born in the Bay of Bengal travel west-north-west along the trough and give much of the rain of Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat.

6.3 The Four IMD Regions

[Correction] The notes list IMD's regions as "South India, Central India, Eastern India, North India". IMD's four homogeneous rainfall regions are North-west India, Central India, South Peninsula, and East and North-east India. "North India" in IMD terms is North-west India (J&K, Ladakh, HP, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh), and "Eastern India" is grouped with the North-east.
IMD regionJune-September LPA (1971-2020)2026 actual2026 % of LPA
North-west India587.6 mm553.0 mm94%
Central India978.0 mm952.8 mm97%
South Peninsula716.2 mm542.0 mm76%
East and North-east India1,367.3 mmabout 1,017 mm74% (lowest since 1901)
All India868.6 mm759.4 mm87% (deficient)

Sources: IMD, Salient Features of the 2026 Southwest Monsoon (30 September 2026); regional LPAs and actual mm from IMD data compiled by NINE145 and FarmingCosmos. IMD gives East and North-east India as 1,017.1 mm in its highlights and the regional table as 1,016.3 mm.

The order of the LPAs is the key revision point: East and North-east (wettest) > Central > South Peninsula > North-west (driest).

6.4 South Peninsula

  • Main source: the Arabian Sea branch. It strikes the Western Ghats almost at right angles; air is forced up the steep western slope and gives very heavy orographic rain - about 250-400 cm a year on the Konkan, Goa, coastal Karnataka and Kerala and the windward slopes (Agumbe, the "Cherrapunji of the South")†.
  • Rain shadow: after crossing the crest the air sinks down the gentle eastern slope, warms by compression and dries. Interior Maharashtra (Pune side, Marathwada), north interior Karnataka and Rayalaseema get less than 50-60 cm†. So rainfall decreases from west to east across the Peninsula, as the notes say.
  • Tamil Nadu in June-September: it lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats, and the Bay of Bengal branch runs parallel to the Coromandel coast, so it gives little rain there ("skips"). Tamil Nadu gets its main rain from the NE monsoon (October-December).

6.5 Central India

  • Arabian Sea branch: one arm enters through the Narmada and Tapi rift valleys (the valleys act as corridors) and gives good rain in the Narmada valley and on the Satpura-Maikal hills.
  • Less rain: the Malwa plateau and Bundelkhand receive less, and Bundelkhand is drought-prone; they lie farther from both branches and are not on the main track of depressions.
  • Bay of Bengal side: the Chhota Nagpur plateau, Chhattisgarh and Odisha get most of their rain from the Bay of Bengal branch and from monsoon depressions moving west-north-west from the Bay. By the time the Narmada-Tapi arm of the Arabian Sea branch reaches Chhota Nagpur it gives only about 15 cm (NCERT)†.
  • 2026 example: Central India was near normal (97% of LPA) and Odisha was the only sub-division with excess rain, because slow-moving Bay depressions repeatedly crossed it (IMD, 30 September 2026).
[Correction] The notes say Chhota Nagpur gets rain from the Bay of Bengal side "and also the north-east branch". The south-west monsoon has no "north-east branch"; its two branches are the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches. Chhota Nagpur's rain comes from the Bay of Bengal branch and Bay depressions. (The north-east monsoon is a different, winter wind system that gives little rain to Chhota Nagpur.)

6.6 East and North-east India

  • Main source: the Bay of Bengal branch, which moves north from the Bay towards Bangladesh and the north-east.
  • Meghalaya: the moist winds are trapped in the funnel-shaped Garo-Khasi-Jaintia hills and forced to rise steeply, giving extreme orographic rain. Mawsynram (East Khasi Hills) holds the WMO record for the highest average annual rainfall: 11,872 mm†. Cherrapunji (Sohra) is close by.
  • Brahmaputra valley gets much less than the surrounding hills (often under 200 cm) - a common trap†.
  • Himalayan foothills: the sub-Himalayan belt of West Bengal, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh gets heavy rain as the winds rise along the mountains.
  • 2026 note: East and North-east India had its lowest June-September rain since 1901 (74% of LPA) in an El Nino year (IMD).

6.7 North-west India: the Ganga Plain and the Thar

  • Purvaiya: the Himalaya deflects the Bay of Bengal branch to the west, so it blows up the Ganga plain as a moist easterly (south-easterly) wind called the purvaiya (purvai), as the notes say.
  • East-to-west decrease: as this branch moves west it loses moisture, so rain decreases from east to west along the plain - NCERT gives about 119 cm at Kolkata, 105 cm at Patna, 76 cm at Prayagraj (Allahabad) and 56 cm at Delhi†.
  • The two branches meet over the north-west Ganga plain and Punjab; the Arabian Sea branch arrives from the south-west and the Bay branch from the east.
  • The Thar (west Rajasthan): the Kutch-Rajasthan arm of the Arabian Sea branch crosses the region parallel to the Aravalli, so nothing forces the air to rise. The very hot land, dry lower air and sinking air aloft (a temperature inversion) also stop clouds from growing. West Rajasthan gets less than 50 cm, Jaisalmer only about 15-20 cm†. Ladakh (Leh) is a cold desert in the rain shadow of the Great Himalaya.
[Correction] The notes head this part "North Indian Ocean". The topic is north India (the northern plains and the north-west), not the ocean. The points under it - east-to-west decrease, the Bay branch skipping the Coromandel coast, and the Thar - belong to the land regions above.
[Correction] The notes explain the dry Thar by "offshore winds". In the monsoon season the winds over Gujarat and Rajasthan are onshore (from the Arabian Sea). The Thar is dry because the Arabian Sea branch runs parallel to the Aravalli and is not lifted, the hot land and sinking air aloft prevent clouds from growing, and the Bay of Bengal branch is exhausted by the time it reaches the far west. "Offshore" winds are the dry winter situation (NE monsoon), not the summer one.

[Current Affairs] Rainfall in 2026.
  • South-west monsoon 2026: 87% of the LPA (759.4 mm) - a deficient season, the 4th lowest since 2001 and 13th lowest since 1901. June was 65% of LPA, July 101%, August 84% and September 92%. 17 of 36 sub-divisions were deficient; only Odisha had excess. Onset over Kerala was on 4 June (3 days late); the whole country was covered by 9 July; withdrawal began on 19 September (IMD, 30 September 2026).
  • Why: a developing and now strong El Nino with a neutral IOD (see the 14 November note on ENSO and IOD). The "monsoon core zone" got 779.9 mm, below the normal range.
  • North-east monsoon 2026: IMD's extended-range forecast of 12 November reported all-India rainfall 32% below normal from 1 October to 11 November. Cyclones Arnab, Murasu and now Akvan have brought bursts of heavy rain mainly to Andhra Pradesh and Telangana rather than to Tamil Nadu (see the 15 November note and IMD extended-range forecast, 12 November 2026).

Key Facts for Prelims

  • Storms of the hot season are low-pressure, convective systems: dust storms (NW), thunderstorms and hail (E, NE, S, central), tropical cyclones (seas).
  • Dust storm = andhi; a wind event (gust front or pressure-gradient wind) over dry, bare soil, April-June, Thar margins.
  • Thunderstorm stages: cumulus → mature → dissipating; the mature stage has both updrafts and downdrafts, an anvil, lightning, hail and a gust front.
  • Thunder = shock wave from air heated by lightning to about 30,000°C, not cloud collision.
  • Lightning deaths 2023 (NCRB): 2,558, about 39.7% of deaths from forces of nature; top states MP 397, Bihar 345, Odisha 294, UP 287, Jharkhand 194.
  • Heat waves and lightning were added to the SDRF/NDRF notified calamities (2026-31).
  • Cyclone conditions: SST above ~26.5-27°C, Coriolis force (rare within ~5° of the equator), low wind shear, a pre-existing low, humid mid-levels, upper divergence.
  • Energy of a tropical cyclone = latent heat of condensation; the eye is calm, clear and warmer than its surroundings.
  • IMD (3-minute sustained wind): D 31-49; DD 50-61; CS 62-88 (named); SCS 89-117; VSCS 118-166; ESCS 167-221; SuCS 222+ km/h.
  • Bay of Bengal cyclone activity is about 4 times the Arabian Sea's; Arabian Sea cyclonic storms rose 52% in frequency and 80% in duration (2001-2019 vs 1982-2000).
  • NIO cyclone seasons: April-May and October-December (post-monsoon more active); few in July-September because of strong wind shear.
  • RSMC New Delhi (IMD) names NIO cyclones; naming since 2004; 13 WMO/ESCAP panel countries; names used in sequence and not reused.
  • Warning stages: pre-cyclone watch, cyclone alert (Orange message), cyclone warning (Red message), post-landfall outlook.
  • 2026 cyclones: Arnab (VSCS, Yanam/AP, 28 Oct; Bangladesh's name), Murasu (SCS, Ongole/AP, 3 Nov; India's name, "drum" in Tamil), Akvan (forecast VSCS, AP coast between Nellore and Tuni, ~20 Nov).
  • Senyar (Nov 2025) - first recorded cyclone to form in the Strait of Malacca.
  • IMD rain normals (1971-2020): annual 1,160.1 mm; SW monsoon 868.6 mm (74.9%); pre-monsoon 130.6 mm; post-monsoon 121.0 mm.
  • IMD regions (Jun-Sep LPA): E&NE 1,367.3 > Central 978.0 > South Peninsula 716.2 > NW 587.6 mm.
  • Tamil Nadu gets about 48% of its annual rain in October-December.
  • Mawsynram: highest average annual rainfall (WMO), 11,872 mm. Rain decreases east to west along the Ganga plain (Kolkata 119, Patna 105, Prayagraj 76, Delhi 56 cm, NCERT).
  • Monsoon 2026: 87% of LPA (deficient); E&NE India lowest since 1901; Odisha the only excess sub-division.

Mains Points

  • Storm types and differences (model answer in 5.1): scale, life, energy source, region, hazard and warning.
  • Why the Bay of Bengal is the cyclone hotspot: warm SST, river-fed fresh layer, seed disturbances, lower shear, funnel shape and shallow shelf for surges; contrast with the Arabian Sea.
  • Climate change and cyclones: more and longer Arabian Sea cyclones, rapid intensification, heavier rain, higher surges on a rising sea; the need to plan for new landfall zones (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka).
  • Cyclone risk reduction: impact-based colour-coded warnings, four-stage warnings, shelters, mangroves, Odisha's zero-casualty model; cascading cyclones (Arnab, Murasu, Akvan) stress state capacity and crops.
  • Lightning as a silent disaster: rural, outdoor victims; early warning (Damini, Sachet), lightning arresters, awareness, and SDRF/NDRF eligibility (2026-31).
  • Regional rainfall: relief, distance from the sea, wind direction, monsoon trough and depressions explain why Mawsynram and Jaisalmer differ a hundredfold; implications for crops, water and drought-proneness (Marathwada, Rayalaseema, Bundelkhand).
  • Monsoon 2026: a deficient El Nino monsoon with record-low rain in the east and north-east - impacts on kharif, reservoirs and rural incomes.

  • Map 2: place the landfalls of Biparjoy (Jakhau), Michaung (Bapatla), Remal (Sagar Island-Khepupara), Dana (Bhitarkanika-Dhamra), Fengal (Puducherry), Montha (Narsapur), Arnab (Yanam), Murasu (Ongole); trace Akvan's forecast track; find the Strait of Malacca (Senyar).
  • Map 3: draw the three arms of the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay branch; mark the Aravalli, the monsoon trough, the >200 cm and <50 cm zones, Mawsynram, Jaisalmer, Leh, Pune, Bengaluru and Chennai.
  • Practise: on an outline map, shade the four IMD regions and write their LPAs; mark Agumbe, Mangaluru, Kolkata, Patna, Prayagraj and Delhi with their rainfall.

Common Traps / Confusions

  • "More than 3 minutes" - wrong. 3 minutes is IMD's averaging period for sustained wind (the US uses 1 minute).
  • VSCS is 118-166 km/h, not 89-167; ESCS is 167-221; SuCS is 222+.
  • A system is named at the cyclonic storm stage (62 km/h), not at depression stage.
  • The eye is warm and calm; the strongest winds are in the eyewall.
  • Thunder is not clouds colliding; it is the sound of lightning-heated air.
  • Bay of Bengal more cyclones - not because it is smaller; because it is warmer, river-freshened and gets seed lows from the east.
  • December cyclones are normal (post-monsoon season is October-December).
  • "More cyclones due to warming" holds for the Arabian Sea, not the whole North Indian Ocean.
  • IMD regions: NW, Central, South Peninsula, East & NE - there is no IMD "North India" or "Eastern India" region.
  • The SW monsoon has no "north-east branch".
  • The Thar is dry because winds are parallel to the Aravalli, not because winds are offshore.
  • Brahmaputra valley gets less than 200 cm even though the hills around it get far more.
  • Tamil Nadu: the NE monsoon (Oct-Dec) is its main rainy season.
  • Annual rain ~116 cm (IMD 1,160.1 mm) vs the SW monsoon LPA ~87 cm (868.6 mm) - do not mix them.

30-Second Revision

Hot land + moisture + trigger → dry NW: andhi | moist E/NE/S: thunderstorm (cumulus → mature → dissipating), lightning, hail | warm sea 26.5-27C + Coriolis + low shear: tropical cyclone
Latent heat → warm core → deeper low → IMD: D 31, DD 50, CS 62 (named), SCS 89, VSCS 118, ESCS 167, SuCS 222 → landfall: wind + rain + surge → Bay 4x Arabian Sea; Arabian Sea +52%
Rain: SW monsoon 75% → relief + distance + direction + trough + depressions → E&NE 1367 > Central 978 > S Pen 716 > NW 588 mm → 2026: 87% (deficient)

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Wording follows the official papers as given in reputable compilations (UnlockIAS, PMF IAS, SuperKalam, WriteUPSC); the official question papers were not opened for this note. Questions marked "near-exact" could not be matched word for word.

1. UPSC CSE Prelims 2015 - General Studies Paper I

In the South Atlantic and South-Eastern Pacific regions in tropical latitudes, cyclone does not originate. What is the reason?

  1. Sea surface temperatures are low
  2. Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone seldom occurs
  3. Coriolis force is too weak
  4. Absence of land in those regions

Answer: (b). Cyclones need a seed disturbance, usually from the ITCZ, which rarely shifts into these regions; cold currents (Benguela, Humboldt) and strong wind shear also inhibit them. Coriolis force is adequate away from the equator, and cyclones form over sea, not land (4.1).

2. UPSC CSE Prelims 2013 - General Studies Paper I

During a thunderstorm, the thunder in the skies is produced by the
1. meeting of cumulonimbus clouds in the sky
2. lightning that separates the nimbus clouds
3. violent upward movement of air and water particles
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.

  1. 1 only
  2. 2 and 3
  3. 1 and 3
  4. None of the above produces the thunder

Answer: (d). Thunder is the shock wave of air heated explosively by lightning (3.3).

3. UPSC CSE Prelims 2020 - General Studies Paper I

Consider the following statements:
1. Jet streams occur in the Northern Hemisphere only.
2. Only some cyclones develop an eye.
3. The temperature inside the eye of a cyclone is nearly 10°C lesser than that of the surroundings.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

  1. 1 only
  2. 2 and 3 only
  3. 2 only
  4. 1 and 3 only

Answer: (c) 2 only. Weaker systems do not form an eye; the eye is warmer than its surroundings (warm core); jet streams occur in both hemispheres (4.2).

4. UPSC CSE Prelims 2013 - General Studies Paper I (near-exact)

The seasonal reversal of winds is the typical characteristic of

  1. Equatorial climate
  2. Mediterranean climate
  3. Monsoon climate
  4. All of the above climates

Answer: (c). The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds; the SW monsoon gives India about 75% of its annual rain, with the regional pattern in section 6.

5. UPSC CSE Mains 2014 - General Studies Paper I (10 marks)

Tropical cyclones are largely confined to South China Sea, Bay of Bengal and Gulf of Mexico. Why?

Approach: list the conditions (warm SST over a deep layer, Coriolis force at 5-20°, low wind shear, seed disturbances from the ITCZ, monsoon trough or easterly waves, high humidity); apply them to these warm, semi-enclosed western basins (Bay of Bengal: fresh-water layer, funnel shape); contrast with cold eastern ocean margins and the South Atlantic; note that the western North Pacific is in fact the most active basin (4.1, 4.5).

6. UPSC CSE Mains 2022 - General Studies Paper I (10 marks)

Discuss the meaning of colour-coded weather warnings for cyclone prone areas given by India Meteorological Department.

Approach: explain Green (no warning), Yellow (be updated), Orange (be prepared), Red (take action); link them to the four-stage cyclone warning (cyclone alert = Orange message, cyclone warning = Red message in current bulletins); give examples (Remal 2024 Red; Akvan 2026 Orange) and the benefits (evacuation, SOPs, resource deployment); conclude with the Sendai Framework's emphasis on early warning (4.7).

7. UPSC CSE Mains 2024 - General Studies Paper I (10 marks)

What is sea surface temperature rise? How does it affect the formation of tropical cyclones?

Approach: define SST and its rise (global warming, marine heatwaves, El Nino/IOD); explain the 26.5°C threshold, latent-heat fuel, ocean heat content and rapid intensification; cite the Arabian Sea trend (+52% frequency, +80% duration) and equatorward genesis; note limits (shear, humidity still matter) (4.8).

8. UPSC CSE Mains 2026 - General Studies Paper I (10 marks)

What is the Fujiwhara effect? Explain its impact on the movement and intensity of tropical cyclones.

Approach: two nearby cyclones rotate about a common centre; tracks bend and speeds change; the stronger may absorb or weaken the other; forecasting becomes harder; give an example of interacting systems (4.4). Question as listed by UnlockIAS; the official paper was not opened.

[No verified PYQ found for this topic] on dust storms or on IMD's four homogeneous rainfall regions specifically.

Corrections Made

Each link returns to the explanation, which keeps the original rough-note claim.

  1. A dust storm is a wind event (gust front or pressure-gradient wind), not a separate low-pressure system.
  2. Thunderstorms and lightning are widespread; central India (MP) had the most lightning deaths in 2023.
  3. Lightning was added to the SDRF/NDRF notified calamities (2026-31), not a "national disaster" list.
  4. IMD bands are CS 62-88, SCS 89-117, VSCS 118-166, ESCS 167-221, SuCS 222+ km/h.
  5. "3 minutes" is the averaging period of sustained wind, not a storm duration.
  6. The Bay's cyclone excess is due to warm, river-freshened water, seed lows and low shear - not its smaller size.
  7. December cyclones belong to the normal post-monsoon season; no evidence they are becoming more frequent.
  8. Cyclone frequency has risen in the Arabian Sea, not across the whole North Indian Ocean.
  9. IMD regions are NW India, Central India, South Peninsula, and East & NE India.
  10. The SW monsoon has no "north-east branch"; Chhota Nagpur's rain comes from the Bay branch and depressions.
  11. The heading "North Indian Ocean" should be north India (the plains and the north-west).
  12. The Thar is dry because the winds run parallel to the Aravalli and sinking air caps convection, not because of offshore winds.
